question: Google University Graduate SWE, initial recruiter call. After basic questions, there was a **rapid-fire round of 7 to 8 questions on Big-O, data structures and algorithms**. Reported examples (the candidate said these were illustrative, not exact): *which is the most inefficient sorting algorithm among insertion, bubble, merge or heap sort*, and *which is better in space complexity, merge sort or heap sort*. The other 5 or 6 questions covered **heaps, priority queues, graphs and self-balancing binary search trees**.
lookingFor: Fast, accurate recall of core complexities, with a one-line justification.
Understanding of average versus worst case, and time versus space.
Knowing why a structure behaves as it does (heap, balanced BST), not just the table.
Clear, concise communication under rapid-fire conditions.
answer:
**Sorting (state worst case and space).**
- Bubble sort: O(n^2) average and worst, O(1) space. Insertion sort: O(n^2) worst but O(n) on nearly sorted input, O(1) space. Both quadratic; bubble sort is generally the slowest in practice because of many swaps, so it is the usual "least efficient" answer.
- Merge sort: O(n log n) in all cases, needs O(n) extra space for arrays (stable).
- Heap sort: O(n log n) worst case, O(1) extra space (in place), not stable.
- So **heap sort has better space complexity than merge sort**. Merge sort is stable and cache-friendly; quicksort (O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst) is usually fastest in practice.

**Heaps and priority queues.** A binary heap is a complete tree in an array; parent is at `(i-1)/2`. Insert and extract-min are O(log n), peek is O(1), and building a heap from n items is O(n) with bottom-up heapify. A priority queue is the abstract type; a heap is the usual implementation. Uses: top-k, Dijkstra, scheduling, merging k sorted lists.

**Graphs.** Adjacency list uses O(V + E) space, a matrix O(V^2). BFS and DFS are O(V + E). Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V), requires non-negative weights. Topological sort works on DAGs; cycle detection through DFS colouring.

**Self-balancing BSTs** (AVL, red-black). They keep height O(log n) with rotations, so search, insert and delete are O(log n) worst case. AVL is more strictly balanced (faster lookups), red-black does fewer rotations on updates. An unbalanced BST degrades to O(n) on sorted input.

**Technique for rapid-fire.** Answer first in one phrase ("heap sort, because it sorts in place"), then give a short reason if there is time. If unsure, say the part you know (for example, the average case) instead of guessing.
followUps: Why is building a heap O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
When would you choose merge sort over quicksort?
How does an AVL tree restore balance after an insertion?
Which sorting algorithms are stable, and why does stability matter?
